placements.title: An autonomous structural parser
placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
The explanation rests on the idea of a parser that deals exclusively with the abstract 
syntactic structure of the sentence (remember the “lumber mill” example from speech 
perception).
The parser has its own operating characteristics. It wants to make the simplest tree possible 
(minimal attachment) and it accomplishes this, in part, by leaving clauses open as long as 
possible (late closure).
This is one way of dealing with ambiguity very efficiently – ignore it until it becomes a 
problem!

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Some problems with a purely syntactic explanation
Syntactically “difficult” sentences aren’t always difficult to parse.
In all of these sentences, 
the verbs in ALL CAPS 
introduce a “reduced 
relative” clause, as in “the 
horse raced past the barn 
fell.”
But these are not 
impossibly difficult 
sentences.
The alternative argument 
advanced by MacDonald, 
Perlmutter & Seidenberg 
(1994), is that semantic 
factors and statistical 
regularities interact with 
“parsing” from very early 
on.

placements.title: Four sentences, four connected lessons
placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Sentence processing in four sentences.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
Syntax is independent of semantics to some extent. In the limit you can have sentences 
that are grammatically correct but meaningless.
The horse raced past the barn fell.
The syntactic structure of a sentence is often highly ambiguous (actually vague), but we 
don’t notice except where things fail. Reading times for “preferred” vs. “unpreferred” 
structures suggest that syntactic processes take shortcuts to save memory, rather than 
activating every possible parse of a sentence.
Put the apple on the towel in the box.
Context, pragmatics, and other factors seem to interact with syntactic processing from 
very early

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
We can see late closure at work 
if we consider a sentence that 
requires the “unpreferred” 
parse to be sensible:
“The burglar blew open the 
safe with the jewels.”
In careful tests of reading time 
and eye movements, we can 
see that people are slower to 
read sentences where the 
sensible reading requires the 
unpreferred parse. 
That is, you momentarily 
entertain the idea that the 
jewels were used to blow open 
the safe, and then have to 
retrace your steps.

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
Another parsing strategy in this 
framework is “late closure.” The 
idea here is that there is a bias 
to keep the current clause 
“open” as long as possible. 
In this case, “with the 
dynamite” wants to associate 
with the big verb phrase 
starting with “blew open.”   
Frazier, L. (1987) Sentence processing: a tutorial 
review, in Attentionand Performance XII: The 
Psychology of Reading (Coltheart, M., ed.),pp. 
559–586, Erlbaum

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
The argument goes that, when we see “Recent research reported by…”
- the fact that “research” is an inanimate object, and unlikely to be the subject of a verb 
like “report” (semantics)
-The fact that “reported” occurs frequently in reduced relatives (lexical statistics) 
- the fact that “reported” occurs very frequently in reduced relatives in scientific papers, 
especially when following the word “research” (lexical statistics and “world knowledge”)
…and many other factors interact with the syntax of the sentence very early on.
Consider:
The burglar arrested in the parking lot was charged today.
The policeman arrested in the parking lot was charged today. 
Why?

Sentence processing in four sentences.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.

that are grammatically correct but meaningless.

structures suggest that syntactic processes take shortcuts to save memory, rather than 
activating every possible parse of a sentence.

very early

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Sentence processing in four sentences.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
Syntax is independent of semantics to some extent. In the limit you can have sentences 
that are grammatically correct but meaningless.
The horse raced past the barn fell.
The syntactic structure of a sentence is often highly ambiguous (actually vague), but we 
don’t notice except where things fail. Reading times for “preferred” vs. “unpreferred” 
structures suggest that syntactic processes take shortcuts to save memory, rather than 
activating every possible parse of a sentence.
Put the apple on the towel in the box.
Context, pragmatics, and other factors seem to interact with syntactic processing from 
very early on.
The bird perches were comfortable.
The very earliest syntactic effects observable in the brain are driven in part by form 
typicality, not necessarily by morphosyntactic structures, and seem to be related to 
predictions about the physical forms of words.

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Man Bites Dog
Why do we need psycholinguistic tests to observe grammatical difficulties in 
comprehension?
In conversation, there are lots of redundant cues to what a speaker intends:
The dog bit the man.
There are so many ways to get the right meaning here:
- Most likely combination of DOG, BITE and MAN into an event representation with 
or without syntax.
- Canonical word order: Agent – Verb – Undergoer; Subject – Verb – Object
Further, a lot of language comprehension takes place in discourse context that clarifies a 
lot...
Maybe Broca’s patients’ comprehension depends on these compensatory heuristics. If 
that were the case you might want to test them with sentences more like:
The dog that the man is biting is angry.

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Some cues to word boundaries
Words sometimes appear in isolation: “Hello.” “No.” “Please.” 
“Go.” “Stop.” etc., but not all words…
Phonotactics: Some sequences of phonemes are very unlikely to 
occur within words: “wordboundary,” “speechcode,” 
“movement.” 
Stress patterns: In English, most words are stressed on the first 
syllable. (Jusczyk et al., 1999)
Kingdom passage
Your kingdom is in a faraway place. The 
prince used to sail to that kingdom when 
he came home from school. One day he 
saw a ghost in this old kingdom…
Device passage
Your device can do a lot. Her device only 
fixes things. My new red device makes ice 
cream. The pink device sews clothes….
7.5 month old Infants familiarized with 
“kingdom” showed a preference for the 
“kingdom” passage.
Infants familiarized with “device” did not show 
the same kind of preference.
In connected speech, stress may help signal 
the beginnings of words. (Of course this won’t 
work in every language, or for every word in 
English!)

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
A generalization test:
If children have really learned the transitive 
structure, they will generalize it to new verbs.
Think about what you need to know in order 
to select the picture that could depict “The 
duck is gorping the bunny” from these two 
novel actions.
Gertner et al (2006) showed that two-year 
olds can understand this: They look 
significantly longer at the duck acting on the 
rabbit than vice-versa.)
At this age, kids typically have a mean length 
of utterance (MLU) of around 2. 
Their three morpheme utterances might be 
like “Duck gorp bunny.”

Participants used the mouse to select the 
picture most consistent with what they 
heard, e.g., a “bear” or a “pear,” just like 
in the experiment you did at home.
A typical, step-like, identification function 
was observed.

placements.title: How a cascade produces the eye-movement result
placements.role: clean word label, not a controlled continuum token
placements.recommendation: Retain only as word-label pronunciation aids; add matched beach–peach and bear–pear continua wherever the manipulated auditory contrast is taught.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
This finding is consistent with the idea that activation flows in a cascaded way from 
features to phonemes.
Even stimuli that are identified as, 
say, /b/, 100% of the time can 
vary in how strongly and 
unambiguously the “voiced” 
feature is activated.
If the stimulus is obviously 
+bilabial and +stop, this creates 
some momentary ambiguity 
between /b/ and /p/.
That ambiguity is reflected in eye-
movements while the participant 
decides where to click.

placements.title: Using eye movements to measure competition
placements.role: clean word label, not a controlled continuum token
placements.recommendation: Retain only as word-label pronunciation aids; add matched beach–peach and bear–pear continua wherever the manipulated auditory contrast is taught.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
McMurray, B., Tanenhaus, M., Aslin, R. and Spivey, M. 
(2003). Probabilistic constraint satisfaction at the 
lexical/phonetic interface: Evidence for gradient effects of 
within-category VOT on lexical access. Journal of 
Psycholinguistic Research, 32, 77-97.
http://www2.psychology.uiowa.edu/faculty/mcmurray/pub
lications/mcmurray-jpr.pdf 
Remember that you’ve seen this kind of 
experiment before, when we talked about 
categorical perception.
Eye movements can tell us about 
competition between possible responses 
participants are considering.
In the McMurray et al. study, the amount of 
competition between BEAR and PEAR 
seemed to depend on distance from the 
category boundary.
Remember?

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A simulation of the Ganong effect in the TRACE model:
As the input unfolds over time, activity accumulates for “plug,” especially when the final /g/ 
arrives, which is highly inconsistent with “blood” and “blush” (also activated in Frame 3).
Thus, this model explains word effects on phoneme category boundaries in terms of top-
down processing. Specifically, activity from the lexical level can produces feedback to the 
phoneme level, producing greater activation for the phoneme consistent with a word.

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A model explaining L1-L2 interactions in terms of spreading activation: 
The Revised Hierarchical Model of Kroll & Stewart (1990; 1994)
Consider what happens in this model when 
performing the Marian & Spivey task in L2:
- the concept for “matches” partially 
activates the Russian word for “matches”
- this activity feeds back to the conceptual 
activation for “matches”
- conceptual activation for “matches” 
leads to eye-movements toward the L1 
competitor.
When the task is done in L1, we might imagine 
that the conceptual links with L2 are too weak 
to create this kind of interference reliably.

primes “queen.”
(the “word -> word” items are things like 
“bill” priming “drug,” etc.)
Thus, it seems that lexical representations 
can be activated even by incomplete

placements.role: vowel-label reference list in distribution context
placements.recommendation: Keep only as label list; do not present neural list as native distribution, Hagiwara sound or Maye exposure.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Remember that formant values are 
partly determined by anatomical 
features that differ between 
speakers of the same language, by 
different rates of speech, and by 
context (e.g., the phones 
produced before and after a 
vowel).  
Nonetheless, formant values can 
provide a pretty good description 
of “vowel space,” especially for a 
specific talker, speaking carefully.
All else being equal, we can produce 
reasonable approximations of 
vowels by manipulating steady-
state formants.

placements.title: Learning a vowel distribution
placements.role: vowel-label reference list in distribution context
placements.recommendation: Keep only as label list; do not present neural list as native distribution, Hagiwara sound or Maye exposure.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Here are the American vowels 
again!
When Kuhl and others talk about 
learning the statistics of 
distributions in the environment, 
they mean things like this.
We can think of a “vowel space” 
determined by the first and second 
formants. 
Maybe we learn the vowels of our 
language by extracting the 
statistics of these distributions.
So, a “prototypical” /a/ is just the 
mean (or mode?) of the 
distribution of all the /a/ sounds 
we hear.

A speech continuum:
These stimuli are 
constructed by 
keeping F1 constant 
and varying F2 onset 
frequency linearly
from stimulus 1 to 13.
Thus: adjacent stimuli 
differ by the same 
amount across the 
entire continuum.

placements.title: The noncategorical prediction for labeling
placements.role: 13step F2 principle and Liberman source experiment
placements.recommendation: Use primary Liberman methods/figure parameters for a clearly labeled reconstruction on experiment pages. Generic sequence may remain only as an explicit equal-F2-step mechanism example. Do not assert its endpoints are /ba/ and /ga/ or boundary locations without validation.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Liberman et al. (1957) available here: http://www.haskins.yale.edu/Reprints/HL0022.pdf
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is non-categorical.
The first thing we’d predict is that categorization 
would get “blurry” as you move away from category 
prototypes. We know the endpoints are /b/ and /g/, 
with /d/ in the middle. Between these points, stimulus 
ambiguity should scale with the distance from the 
prototype. So, stimulus 2 would be 75/25 /b/ - /d/.

placements.title: The noncategorical prediction for discrimination
placements.role: 13step F2 principle and Liberman source experiment
placements.recommendation: Use primary Liberman methods/figure parameters for a clearly labeled reconstruction on experiment pages. Generic sequence may remain only as an explicit equal-F2-step mechanism example. Do not assert its endpoints are /ba/ and /ga/ or boundary locations without validation.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is linear.
But the other important thing we’d predict is that Discrimination performance should 
be independent of Labeling. 
Obviously labeling has to have a sort of “peaked” function, because you’ve got three 
categories, and you’re asking people to make binary responses. But for the 
discrimination task, you’re just asking people to say “same” or “different.” If 
perception of differences in F2 onset were constant over the whole continuum, 
discrimination accuracy would also be constant.

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A speech continuum:
These stimuli are 
constructed by 
keeping F1 constant 
and varying F2 onset 
frequency linearly
from stimulus 1 to 13.
Thus: adjacent stimuli 
differ by the same 
amount across the 
entire continuum.

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Liberman et al. (1957) available here: http://www.haskins.yale.edu/Reprints/HL0022.pdf
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is non-categorical.
The first thing we’d predict is that categorization 
would get “blurry” as you move away from category 
prototypes. We know the endpoints are /b/ and /g/, 
with /d/ in the middle. Between these points, stimulus 
ambiguity should scale with the distance from the 
prototype. So, stimulus 2 would be 75/25 /b/ - /d/.

placements.role: 13step F2 principle and Liberman source experiment
placements.recommendation: Use primary Liberman methods/figure parameters for a clearly labeled reconstruction on experiment pages. Generic sequence may remain only as an explicit equal-F2-step mechanism example. Do not assert its endpoints are /ba/ and /ga/ or boundary locations without validation.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is linear.
But the other important thing we’d predict is that Discrimination performance should 
be independent of Labeling. 
Obviously labeling has to have a sort of “peaked” function, because you’ve got three 
categories, and you’re asking people to make binary responses. But for the 
discrimination task, you’re just asking people to say “same” or “different.” If 
perception of differences in F2 onset were constant over the whole continuum, 
discrimination accuracy would also be constant.

placements.title: How a cascade produces the eye-movement result
placements.role: lexical continuum or visual-world VOT study
placements.recommendation: Replace with word-matched beach–peach or bear–pear continuum for this source slide, preserving common rhyme and manipulated onset.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
This finding is consistent with the idea that activation flows in a cascaded way from 
features to phonemes.
Even stimuli that are identified as, 
say, /b/, 100% of the time can 
vary in how strongly and 
unambiguously the “voiced” 
feature is activated.
If the stimulus is obviously 
+bilabial and +stop, this creates 
some momentary ambiguity 
between /b/ and /p/.
That ambiguity is reflected in eye-
movements while the participant 
decides where to click.

clips.title: Frequency-matched teaching stream
clips.current_scope: Illustrative new stimulus construction. Uses the source slide’s exact displayed sequence, not a claim that these are the original 1996 recordings. source_proof.summary: Displayed development2 pages6–9 exact toy strings crosschecked against saffran_source_inventory.json and build_saffran.py.135syllables at250ms,160Hz/equalRMS/no added gaps; shortstream30syllables includes gopila and bugiko twice each.
source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Testing for an effect of transitional 
probabilities
After listening to a long stream of syllables, it’s trivial to show that infants are 
more familiar with sequences they have heard than ones they haven’t.
Two additional details are important:
1. Half of the words were repeated more frequently than the other half.
2. Test for familiarity was against “part words” that were matched for 
frequency of occurrence with real words.
Example:
tokibu gikoba gopila gikoba tokibu gopila tokibu gikoba gikoba tokibu
Here GOPILA and BU-GIKO both appear twice, but the probability of GI given BU is 
2/4, whereas the TPs for GOPILA are both 2/2.
source_proof.exact_input_text: tokibu gikoba gopila gikoba tokibu gopila tokibu gikoba gikoba tokibu

clips.recommendation: Retain clear source-slide reconstruction wording. Do not label tokibu/gikoba/gopila/tipolu as exact historical1996 stimulus words, and do not equate33.75s classroom stream with full infant familiarization.

placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Listen to sounds from many, many languages here: http://archive.phonetics.ucla.edu/
We’ve talked a lot about 
categorical perception and the 
notion of acquired similarity for 
sounds in the same category.
Here are some minimal pairs in 
Hindi. 
Native English speakers tend to 
use our “alveolar” category to 
interpret both dental and 
retroflex consonants.
So in this case, transfer makes 
learning the L2 contrast more 
difficult. 
Transfer and phonetic/phonological learning

placements.recommendation: Label Russian competitor pronunciation for reference; this competitor was not an additional spoken item in the illustrated English-target trial.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
When only one competitor was present, participants made eye movements to both within- and 
between-language competitors to the same extent.
When both within- and between-language competitors were present, participants looked at the 
within-language competitor more, but still looked at the between-language competitor a lot 
(i.e., twice as often as a control condition).
Competition during L2 spoken word recognition

placements.title: The asymmetry during L1 processing
placements.role: Russian spoken auditory target, matches, in L1 condition
placements.recommendation: Retain this Russian word but label it the Russian-language auditory TARGET. It is the unspoken competitor only on the English speaker trial. Original page17 table establishes both roles.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
In contrast, English words do not seem to be activated when (native Russian speakers) do this 
experiment in Russian.
(The small numerical difference between the between-language and control conditions is not 
statistically significant.)
Competition during L1 spoken word recognition

placements.title: How a competitor gains conceptual support
placements.role: activated pictured Russian competitor, not played English-target word
placements.recommendation: Label Russian competitor pronunciation for reference; this competitor was not an additional spoken item in the illustrated English-target trial.
placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A model explaining L1-L2 interactions in terms of spreading activation: 
The Revised Hierarchical Model of Kroll & Stewart (1990; 1994)
Consider what happens in this model when 
performing the Marian & Spivey task in L2:
- the concept for “matches” partially 
activates the Russian word for “matches”
- this activity feeds back to the conceptual 
activation for “matches”
- conceptual activation for “matches” 
leads to eye-movements toward the L1 
competitor.
When the task is done in L1, we might imagine 
that the conceptual links with L2 are too weak 
to create this kind of interference reliably.

placements.role: activated pictured Russian competitor, not played English-target word

placements.original_slide_excerpt:

Hypothesis: If L1 words are always activated, native Russian speakers should look at,

source_proof.anchor_original_source_text:
Another example where transfer causes 
problems is with grammatical gender.
Grammatical gender is different from 
social/cultural gender.
There’s nothing “male” about a book or 
“female” about liberty (although: hold that 
thought for when we discuss “language and 
thought” later in the semester).
But grammatical gender has implications for 
agreement. Pronouns, adjectives, some forms of 
verb, etc. all need to be coordinated with noun 
gender.
French is famous for having synonyms with different gender:
auto/voiture
rivière/fleuve
vélo/bicyclette
source_proof.frontend_phonemes: otˈo

all_placements.title: An autonomous structural parser
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
The explanation rests on the idea of a parser that deals exclusively with the abstract 
syntactic structure of the sentence (remember the “lumber mill” example from speech 
perception).
The parser has its own operating characteristics. It wants to make the simplest tree possible 
(minimal attachment) and it accomplishes this, in part, by leaving clauses open as long as 
possible (late closure).
This is one way of dealing with ambiguity very efficiently – ignore it until it becomes a 
problem!

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Some problems with a purely syntactic explanation
Syntactically “difficult” sentences aren’t always difficult to parse.
In all of these sentences, 
the verbs in ALL CAPS 
introduce a “reduced 
relative” clause, as in “the 
horse raced past the barn 
fell.”
But these are not 
impossibly difficult 
sentences.
The alternative argument 
advanced by MacDonald, 
Perlmutter & Seidenberg 
(1994), is that semantic 
factors and statistical 
regularities interact with 
“parsing” from very early 
on.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Sentence processing in four sentences.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
Syntax is independent of semantics to some extent. In the limit you can have sentences 
that are grammatically correct but meaningless.
The horse raced past the barn fell.
The syntactic structure of a sentence is often highly ambiguous (actually vague), but we 
don’t notice except where things fail. Reading times for “preferred” vs. “unpreferred” 
structures suggest that syntactic processes take shortcuts to save memory, rather than 
activating every possible parse of a sentence.
Put the apple on the towel in the box.
Context, pragmatics, and other factors seem to interact with syntactic processing from 
very early

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
Another parsing strategy in this 
framework is “late closure.” The 
idea here is that there is a bias 
to keep the current clause 
“open” as long as possible. 
In this case, “with the 
dynamite” wants to associate 
with the big verb phrase 
starting with “blew open.”   
Frazier, L. (1987) Sentence processing: a tutorial 
review, in Attentionand Performance XII: The 
Psychology of Reading (Coltheart, M., ed.),pp. 
559–586, Erlbaum

all_placements.title: Why jewels create a processing cost
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
We can see late closure at work 
if we consider a sentence that 
requires the “unpreferred” 
parse to be sensible:
“The burglar blew open the 
safe with the jewels.”
In careful tests of reading time 
and eye movements, we can 
see that people are slower to 
read sentences where the 
sensible reading requires the 
unpreferred parse. 
That is, you momentarily 
entertain the idea that the 
jewels were used to blow open 
the safe, and then have to 
retrace your steps.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
Another parsing strategy in this 
framework is “late closure.” The 
idea here is that there is a bias 
to keep the current clause 
“open” as long as possible. 
In this case, “with the 
dynamite” wants to associate 
with the big verb phrase 
starting with “blew open.”   
Frazier, L. (1987) Sentence processing: a tutorial 
review, in Attentionand Performance XII: The 
Psychology of Reading (Coltheart, M., ed.),pp. 
559–586, Erlbaum

all_placements.title: Why jewels create a processing cost
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Syntactic explanations of the “garden path” effect
We can see late closure at work 
if we consider a sentence that 
requires the “unpreferred” 
parse to be sensible:
“The burglar blew open the 
safe with the jewels.”
In careful tests of reading time 
and eye movements, we can 
see that people are slower to 
read sentences where the 
sensible reading requires the 
unpreferred parse. 
That is, you momentarily 
entertain the idea that the 
jewels were used to blow open 
the safe, and then have to 
retrace your steps.

all_placements.title: Research reported and the arrested burglar
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
The argument goes that, when we see “Recent research reported by…”
- the fact that “research” is an inanimate object, and unlikely to be the subject of a verb 
like “report” (semantics)
-The fact that “reported” occurs frequently in reduced relatives (lexical statistics) 
- the fact that “reported” occurs very frequently in reduced relatives in scientific papers, 
especially when following the word “research” (lexical statistics and “world knowledge”)
…and many other factors interact with the syntax of the sentence very early on.
Consider:
The burglar arrested in the parking lot was charged today.
The policeman arrested in the parking lot was charged today. 
Why?

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Sentence processing in four sentences.
Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.
Syntax is independent of semantics to some extent. In the limit you can have sentences 
that are grammatically correct but meaningless.
The horse raced past the barn fell.
The syntactic structure of a sentence is often highly ambiguous (actually vague), but we 
don’t notice except where things fail. Reading times for “preferred” vs. “unpreferred” 
structures suggest that syntactic processes take shortcuts to save memory, rather than 
activating every possible parse of a sentence.
Put the apple on the towel in the box.
Context, pragmatics, and other factors seem to interact with syntactic processing from 
very early

all_placements.title: Spivey: an apple, a towel, and a box
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as new readings; label the wording separately from the original method. For ambiguous strings say prosody is model-generated. Do not imply these are original experiment recordings.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
“World knowledge” can be very local
Spivey et al. (1995) gave people a visual world with 
a pencil, a box, a towel and an apple on a towel.
People were then instructed to “put the apple on 
the towel in the box.”
You can imagine that with minimal attachment, 
“the towel” would temporarily seem like it should 
be the end of the clause “put the apple on the 
towel.” 
And lo, people do seem to look at the towel while 
planning their movements, as though they are 
considering it as a target, before planning a 
movement to the box.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Psychophysiological investigations of syntax.
The early left anterior negativity 
(ELAN) is an ERP phenomenon 
elicited for word class violations.
Some classic ELAN stimuli:
The pizza was in the eaten.
The scientist criticized Max’s of
proof the theorem.
Features of the ELAN:
- early (100-200ms)
- left/anterior (language-
specific?)
- specifically for word category
violations, i.e., a noun when a verb is 
expected, or a preposition.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Some cues to word boundaries
Words sometimes appear in isolation: “Hello.” “No.” “Please.” 
“Go.” “Stop.” etc., but not all words…
Phonotactics: Some sequences of phonemes are very unlikely to 
occur within words: “wordboundary,” “speechcode,” 
“movement.” 
Stress patterns: In English, most words are stressed on the first 
syllable. (Jusczyk et al., 1999)

prince used to sail to that kingdom when 
he came home from school. One day he 
saw a ghost in this old kingdom…
Device passage
Your device can do a lot. Her device only 
fixes things. My new red device makes ice 
cream. The pink device sews clothes….

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Statistical learning of word segmentation 
from transitional probabilities
Another cue to word boundaries. 
Consider: “Pretty baby.”
When you look at English words, the syllable   
/ti/ is very strongly predicted by the syllable 
/prI/, but this is less likely to be true for 
syllable pairs across words:
(freq) pretty
(freq) pre
(freq) tyba
(freq) ty

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
How do children start putting words together?
In production, it can be difficult to distinguish what’s going on when children produce only 
one, two or three words at a time.
Menn distinguishes among:
- “just a bunch of relevant words”
- formulas
- word combinations
- stable constructions (not necessarily adult-like)
Up!
Pick you up!
Mommy up!
In practice, a full description of the context in 
which an utterance is produced is necessary 
(but often not sufficient!) to distinguish among 
these.

all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as printed-example readings. Identify kingdom/device audio as displayed excerpt rather than complete original familiarization. Do not use the model prosody as evidence of segmentation performance.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A generalization test:
If children have really learned the transitive 
structure, they will generalize it to new verbs.
Think about what you need to know in order 
to select the picture that could depict “The 
duck is gorping the bunny” from these two 
novel actions.
Gertner et al (2006) showed that two-year 
olds can understand this: They look 
significantly longer at the duck acting on the 
rabbit than vice-versa.)
At this age, kids typically have a mean length 
of utterance (MLU) of around 2. 
Their three morpheme utterances might be 
like “Duck gorp bunny.”

(lumber mill) or cascaded (food web) processing?

all_placements.title: How a cascade produces the eye-movement result
all_placements.role: clean word label, not a controlled continuum token
all_placements.recommendation: Retain only as word-label pronunciation aids; add matched beach–peach and bear–pear continua wherever the manipulated auditory contrast is taught.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
This finding is consistent with the idea that activation flows in a cascaded way from 
features to phonemes.
Even stimuli that are identified as, 
say, /b/, 100% of the time can 
vary in how strongly and 
unambiguously the “voiced” 
feature is activated.
If the stimulus is obviously 
+bilabial and +stop, this creates 
some momentary ambiguity 
between /b/ and /p/.
That ambiguity is reflected in eye-
movements while the participant 
decides where to click.

all_placements.title: Why the final /g/ favors plug
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain as candidate pronunciations. Label that the model considers alternatives as /plug/ unfolds; do not make a three-word playback look like original input.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A simulation of the Ganong effect in the TRACE model:
As the input unfolds over time, activity accumulates for “plug,” especially when the final /g/ 
arrives, which is highly inconsistent with “blood” and “blush” (also activated in Frame 3).
Thus, this model explains word effects on phoneme category boundaries in terms of top-
down processing. Specifically, activity from the lexical level can produces feedback to the 
phoneme level, producing greater activation for the phoneme consistent with a word.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A model explaining L1-L2 interactions in terms of spreading activation: 
The Revised Hierarchical Model of Kroll & Stewart (1990; 1994)
Consider what happens in this model when 
performing the Marian & Spivey task in L2:
- the concept for “matches” partially 
activates the Russian word for “matches”
- this activity feeds back to the conceptual 
activation for “matches”
- conceptual activation for “matches” 
leads to eye-movements toward the L1 
competitor.
When the task is done in L1, we might imagine 
that the conceptual links with L2 are too weak 
to create this kind of interference reliably.

all_placements.title: Stop consonants and formant transitions
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Keep as separate clean category pronunciations. Use primary-source continuum for the manipulation, with no claim that these TTS endpoints establish the category boundaries of the acoustic-model sequence.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Liberman et al. (1957) available here: http://www.haskins.yale.edu/Reprints/HL0022.pdf
Stop consonants are 
distinguished by 
formant transitions. 
This is sensible if you 
think about how 
they’re produced: the 
audible part of a /b/, 
/d/, or /g/, happens 
while your jaw is 
opening.
The pattern playback 
synthesizer was used 
to create speech-like 
sounds that replicated 
these formant 
transitions.

constructed by 
keeping F1 constant

from stimulus 1 to 13.

entire continuum.

all_placements.title: Vowel space contains distributions
all_placements.role: vowel-label reference list in distribution context
all_placements.recommendation: Keep only as label list; do not present neural list as native distribution, Hagiwara sound or Maye exposure.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Remember that formant values are 
partly determined by anatomical 
features that differ between 
speakers of the same language, by 
different rates of speech, and by 
context (e.g., the phones 
produced before and after a 
vowel).  
Nonetheless, formant values can 
provide a pretty good description 
of “vowel space,” especially for a 
specific talker, speaking carefully.
All else being equal, we can produce 
reasonable approximations of 
vowels by manipulating steady-
state formants.

all_placements.title: Learning a vowel distribution
all_placements.role: vowel-label reference list in distribution context
all_placements.recommendation: Keep only as label list; do not present neural list as native distribution, Hagiwara sound or Maye exposure.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Here are the American vowels 
again!
When Kuhl and others talk about 
learning the statistics of 
distributions in the environment, 
they mean things like this.
We can think of a “vowel space” 
determined by the first and second 
formants. 
Maybe we learn the vowels of our 
language by extracting the 
statistics of these distributions.
So, a “prototypical” /a/ is just the 
mean (or mode?) of the 
distribution of all the /a/ sounds 
we hear.

all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain the new mechanism demonstration with numerical F1/F2 labels. On a vowel-distribution slide distinguish an example filter change from observed population/distribution data.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Let’s learn about formants by doing some 
source-filter synthesis
(I did all of this with Praat free software for speech analysis, available at praat.org)
This is a spectrogram of me 
saying /u/.
I’ve got the cursor on the 
first formant, you can 
see it’s at about 300Hz.
The second formant is very 
low, around 900Hz.

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Let’s learn about formants by doing some 
source-filter synthesis
Actually, Praat can 
automatically find 
formants. 
Here it’s identified five. 
Only the first three are 
usually important for 
phonemic processing.
In this example, we’ll only 
deal with the first two.

all_placements.title: Separating the source from the filter
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain the new mechanism demonstration with numerical F1/F2 labels. On a vowel-distribution slide distinguish an example filter change from observed population/distribution data.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
This is the source…
So, now what I’ve done is 
extract the SOURCE from 
the sound, using a model 
of the filter based on the 
formant frequencies.
(This is a little bit like doing 
a multiple regression 
analysis.)
The result is a more-or-less 
“unfiltered” version of 
my voice. It sounds like a 
buzz…

all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Liberman et al. (1957) available here: http://www.haskins.yale.edu/Reprints/HL0022.pdf
Stop consonants are 
distinguished by 
formant transitions. 
This is sensible if you 
think about how 
they’re produced: the 
audible part of a /b/, 
/d/, or /g/, happens 
while your jaw is 
opening.
The pattern playback 
synthesizer was used 
to create speech-like 
sounds that replicated 
these formant 
transitions.

all_placements.title: The noncategorical prediction for labeling
all_placements.role: 13step F2 principle and Liberman source experiment
all_placements.recommendation: Use primary Liberman methods/figure parameters for a clearly labeled reconstruction on experiment pages. Generic sequence may remain only as an explicit equal-F2-step mechanism example. Do not assert its endpoints are /ba/ and /ga/ or boundary locations without validation.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Liberman et al. (1957) available here: http://www.haskins.yale.edu/Reprints/HL0022.pdf
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is non-categorical.
The first thing we’d predict is that categorization 
would get “blurry” as you move away from category 
prototypes. We know the endpoints are /b/ and /g/, 
with /d/ in the middle. Between these points, stimulus 
ambiguity should scale with the distance from the 
prototype. So, stimulus 2 would be 75/25 /b/ - /d/.

all_placements.title: The noncategorical prediction for discrimination
all_placements.role: 13step F2 principle and Liberman source experiment
all_placements.recommendation: Use primary Liberman methods/figure parameters for a clearly labeled reconstruction on experiment pages. Generic sequence may remain only as an explicit equal-F2-step mechanism example. Do not assert its endpoints are /ba/ and /ga/ or boundary locations without validation.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A simple “ideal observer” model assuming perception 
is linear.
But the other important thing we’d predict is that Discrimination performance should 
be independent of Labeling. 
Obviously labeling has to have a sort of “peaked” function, because you’ve got three 
categories, and you’re asking people to make binary responses. But for the 
discrimination task, you’re just asking people to say “same” or “different.” If 
perception of differences in F2 onset were constant over the whole continuum, 
discrimination accuracy would also be constant.

all_placements.title: How a cascade produces the eye-movement result
all_placements.role: lexical continuum or visual-world VOT study
all_placements.recommendation: Replace with word-matched beach–peach or bear–pear continuum for this source slide, preserving common rhyme and manipulated onset.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
This finding is consistent with the idea that activation flows in a cascaded way from 
features to phonemes.
Even stimuli that are identified as, 
say, /b/, 100% of the time can 
vary in how strongly and 
unambiguously the “voiced” 
feature is activated.
If the stimulus is obviously 
+bilabial and +stop, this creates 
some momentary ambiguity 
between /b/ and /p/.
That ambiguity is reflected in eye-
movements while the participant 
decides where to click.

Psycholinguistic Research, 32, 77-97.
http://www2.psychology.uiowa.edu/faculty/mcmurray/pub
lications/mcmurray-jpr.pdf 
Remember that you’ve seen this kind of 
experiment before, when we talked about 
categorical perception.
Eye movements can tell us about 
competition between possible responses 
participants are considering.
In the McMurray et al. study, the amount of 
competition between BEAR and PEAR 
seemed to depend on distance from the 
category boundary.
Remember?

Isolating statistical information from 
other cues (Saffran et al., 1996)
In order to show that transitional probabilities can 
be used to identify words, stimuli were tightly 
controlled:
monotone (no changes in pitch, duration, amplitude, etc.)
simple CV syllables (no phonotactic cues to word boundaries)
presented continuously (no pauses)
A set of three-syllable “words” was created, (e.g., 
tokibu, gikoba, gopila)

all_placements.title: Words versus frequency-matched part-words
all_placements.role: controlled reconstruction of source slide toy sequence, not full historical familiarization
all_placements.recommendation: Retain clear source-slide reconstruction wording. Do not label tokibu/gikoba/gopila/tipolu as exact historical1996 stimulus words, and do not equate33.75s classroom stream with full infant familiarization.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Testing for an effect of transitional 
probabilities
After listening to a long stream of syllables, it’s trivial to show that infants are 
more familiar with sequences they have heard than ones they haven’t.
Two additional details are important:
1. Half of the words were repeated more frequently than the other half.
2. Test for familiarity was against “part words” that were matched for 
frequency of occurrence with real words.
Example:
tokibu gikoba gopila gikoba tokibu gopila tokibu gikoba gikoba tokibu
Here GOPILA and BU-GIKO both appear twice, but the probability of GI given BU is 
2/4, whereas the TPs for GOPILA are both 2/2.

all_placements.role: activated pictured Russian competitor, not played English-target word
all_placements.recommendation: Label Russian competitor pronunciation for reference; this competitor was not an additional spoken item in the illustrated English-target trial.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Marian & Spivey examined the cohort effect with “cross-language competitors”
Hypothesis: If L1 words are always activated, native Russian speakers should look at, 
e.g., a book of matches when the target is “speaker” in English.

all_placements.title: Competition during L2 processing
all_placements.role: activated pictured Russian competitor, not played English-target word
all_placements.recommendation: Label Russian competitor pronunciation for reference; this competitor was not an additional spoken item in the illustrated English-target trial.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
When only one competitor was present, participants made eye movements to both within- and 
between-language competitors to the same extent.
When both within- and between-language competitors were present, participants looked at the 
within-language competitor more, but still looked at the between-language competitor a lot 
(i.e., twice as often as a control condition).
Competition during L2 spoken word recognition

all_placements.title: The asymmetry during L1 processing
all_placements.role: Russian spoken auditory target, matches, in L1 condition
all_placements.recommendation: Retain this Russian word but label it the Russian-language auditory TARGET. It is the unspoken competitor only on the English speaker trial. Original page17 table establishes both roles.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
In contrast, English words do not seem to be activated when (native Russian speakers) do this 
experiment in Russian.
(The small numerical difference between the between-language and control conditions is not 
statistically significant.)
Competition during L1 spoken word recognition

all_placements.title: How a competitor gains conceptual support
all_placements.role: activated pictured Russian competitor, not played English-target word
all_placements.recommendation: Label Russian competitor pronunciation for reference; this competitor was not an additional spoken item in the illustrated English-target trial.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
A model explaining L1-L2 interactions in terms of spreading activation: 
The Revised Hierarchical Model of Kroll & Stewart (1990; 1994)
Consider what happens in this model when 
performing the Marian & Spivey task in L2:
- the concept for “matches” partially 
activates the Russian word for “matches”
- this activity feeds back to the conceptual 
activation for “matches”
- conceptual activation for “matches” 
leads to eye-movements toward the L1 
competitor.
When the task is done in L1, we might imagine 
that the conceptual links with L2 are too weak 
to create this kind of interference reliably.

all_placements.title: Grammatical gender and agreement
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain model-language/word label. Narrow cognate page8 to its actual French words auto, rivière and bicyclette unless expressly labeling prior-page lexical context.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Another example where transfer causes 
problems is with grammatical gender.
Grammatical gender is different from 
social/cultural gender.
There’s nothing “male” about a book or 
“female” about liberty (although: hold that 
thought for when we discuss “language and 
thought” later in the semester).
But grammatical gender has implications for 
agreement. Pronouns, adjectives, some forms of 
verb, etc. all need to be coordinated with noun 
gender.
French is famous for having synonyms with different gender:
auto/voiture
rivière/fleuve
vélo/bicyclette

all_placements.title: Grammatical gender and agreement
all_placements.role: source example or study-linked explanatory context
all_placements.recommendation: Retain model-language/word label. Narrow cognate page8 to its actual French words auto, rivière and bicyclette unless expressly labeling prior-page lexical context.
all_placements.original_slide_excerpt:
Another example where transfer causes 
problems is with grammatical gender.
Grammatical gender is different from 
social/cultural gender.
There’s nothing “male” about a book or 
“female” about liberty (although: hold that 
thought for when we discuss “language and 
thought” later in the semester).
But grammatical gender has implications for 
agreement. Pronouns, adjectives, some forms of 
verb, etc. all need to be coordinated with noun 
gender.
French is famous for having synonyms with different gender:
auto/voiture
rivière/fleuve
vélo/bicyclette

“Arnold esta embarazado.”

The bias to interpret L2 words as related to
